title: US telephone switching: delayed automation, displaced incumbents and later entrants
summary: Mechanical switching required a service system to change, while the labour consequences differed between incumbent operators and subsequent entrants. The study is a bounded counterexample to inferring individual opportunity from aggregate employment resilience.

stages.invention: Mechanical switching existed by the 1880s in the author-summary account.
stages.feasibility: Feasible apparatus did not establish viability across AT&T’s interdependent service system.
stages.deployment: AT&T began automating in the late 1910s; local cutovers provide study timing.
stages.diffusion: Over half the US network was converted during 1920–1940 according to the study; not every exchange at once.
stages.scaling: Technical change, system adaptation and market scale enter the authors’ account; their relative weights are not adjudicated here.
stages.non-adoption: Smaller/manual exchanges persisted; exact service-area comparison requires full adoption-paper audit.
stages.displacement: Operators’ tasks were displaced, with separate outcomes for incumbents and future cohorts.

counterevidence: No overall employment decline for later cohorts does not erase incumbent loss; limited-power wage tests cannot establish unchanged earnings.

episode.technology_configuration: Mechanical local call switching replacing manual operator switching in US exchanges
episode.task: Connect telephone calls within an interdependent service network
episode.population: Adopting exchanges; main later-cohort results for white American-born women aged 16–25 in smaller US cities; separate linked incumbent sample
contemporary_alternatives: Hybrid/manual service in other exchanges or tasks
episode.adoption_measure: Exchange cutover timing and network penetration; census employment/occupation and selected wage outcomes. Cohort and incumbent denominators differ.
episode.observation_limits: Newspaper coverage and genealogical linkage are selective; census decade intervals obscure short transitions; occupational scores are not each individual’s observed pay.

actors.chooser: Telephone company management selected system adoption and exchange cutovers.
actors.payer: Company investment funded through business revenues/capital; precise incidence on subscribers not estimated here.
actors.operator_maintainer: Operators, switching technicians and service staff; task balance changes.
actors.affected_nonchooser: Displaced operators, prospective entrants and subscribers.
actors.ability_to_refuse: Workers did not individually control equipment replacement; ability to move into alternative employment varied. No comprehensive measure of refusal rights or bargaining acquired.

labour.tasks: Manual switching displaced; other clerical/service work expanded for later entrants.
labour.entry_barriers: Gender/racial hiring boundaries and occupational skills matter; main sample excludes many groups, so equal accessibility is not established. Technicians were nearly all male, and the successive young-female-cohort analysis does not find a rise in other telephone employment after cutover (LBR-K08); this is not a ban on every individual transition.
labour.bargaining_ownership: Company ownership controlled automation; causal effect of bargaining arrangements not established.
labour.transition: Incumbents tracked a decade later; future cohorts observed separately. Short unemployment spells incompletely captured.
labour.distribution: Incumbents versus later cohorts diverge; racial/immigrant populations cannot be collapsed into main estimates.
labour.evidence_limit: No proof that every displaced worker could enter the growing roles, or that aggregate gains compensated losses.

title: US new job specialties and innovation, 1940–2018
summary: A longitudinal title-based study documents new work and connects it with innovation and demand. Its measurement is informative but cannot be converted directly into a count of technology-created jobs or a forecast of opportunity.

stages.invention: Study uses patent-based exposure as one innovation measure, not a list of first inventions.
stages.feasibility: Not directly measured for each technology.
stages.deployment: Patent exposure is not equivalent to installed adoption.
stages.diffusion: Occupational title emergence and employment composition are observed/imputed; no universal technology adoption rate.
stages.scaling: Aggregate employment allocation changes over decades.
stages.non-adoption: Inventions not patented and work not captured by title revisions remain partly unobserved.
stages.displacement: Automation and new tasks can operate simultaneously and affect different occupations.

counterevidence: New titles can reflect classification changes; patents miss innovation and expose the same occupation to both automation and augmentation.

episode.technology_configuration: Multiple innovation exposures matched to US occupational tasks and outputs; a comparative data study rather than one device
episode.task: Measure creation and reorganisation of job specialties
episode.population: US census occupations and employed population, 1940–2018; micro-title counts do not directly enumerate workers
episode.adoption_measure: New Census Alphabetical Index titles; imputed employment shares; patent-to-task/output similarity exposures. These are distinct proxies.
episode.observation_limits: Title-based imputation, changing classifications and incomplete patent coverage; no universal count of new occupations or technology-caused employment.

actors.chooser: Firms, customers and workers jointly shape tasks; census classification is an observation institution.
actors.payer: Employers and buyers fund paid work; unpaid work is outside the principal measurement.
actors.operator_maintainer: Workers in changing occupational task bundles.
actors.affected_nonchooser: Workers losing tasks or excluded from new specialties.
actors.ability_to_refuse: Not identified at individual level in these aggregate data.

labour.tasks: Creation and displacement can coexist within and across occupations.
labour.entry_barriers: Education, skills, resources and discrimination are not fully identified by title counts.
labour.bargaining_ownership: Distribution of task value between owners and workers is not recovered from title emergence alone.
labour.transition: Decadal aggregate patterns; individual mobility into new work not directly established.
labour.distribution: Composition shifted across pay/skill groups; no guarantee of equal access.
labour.evidence_limit: US historical patterns do not forecast occupations, net employment or accessible gains for a present individual.
